messages.claude:
feat: support `scaled_dot_product_attention` and `__matmul__` in FLOPS Profiler

What:
- Add `_attn_flops_compute` to compute MACs for `F.scaled_dot_product_attention`,
  accounting for both the QK^T matmul (q.shape * k.seq_len) and the softmax·V
  matmul (q.shape[:-1] * k.seq_len * v.feature_dim).
- Register `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` in `_patch_functionals` via `wrapFunc`.
- Patch `torch.Tensor.__matmul__` in `_patch_tensor_methods` so expressions like
  `a @ b` are counted in addition to the existing `torch.matmul`/`mm`/`bmm` paths.

Why:
- The FLOPS profiler silently skipped `F.scaled_dot_product_attention`, the
  primary attention path used by modern transformer models, so reported flops
  were significantly understated for any model relying on fused SDPA kernels.
- The `a @ b` operator form (`__matmul__`) was likewise uninstrumented, causing
  flops to be missed for code written with the `@` operator even though the
  explicit `torch.matmul`/`mm`/`bmm` calls were already covered. This resolves
  issue #4723 by ensuring both the fused attention op and the operator-form
  matmul are reflected in profiling results.

fix: resolve circular import during pip install by deferring torch imports

The changes defer torch imports from module load time to runtime in XPU op builders. This fixes issue #4984 where `pip install deepspeed==0.13.0` fails with ImportError during egg_info preparation. The error occurred because TORCH_MAJOR/TORCH_MINOR were imported at module level before torch was available, and async_io.py imported torch unconditionally at the top. By moving these imports into the methods that use them (cxx_args and version_dependent_macros), the build can proceed without requiring torch as a build-time dependency.
messages.claude:
fix: resolve deepspeed 0.13.0 install failure caused by torch import at module load

Move the `import torch` in `op_builder/xpu/async_io.py` from module top-level into `cxx_args()` so it is only required at JIT build time, not at package import time. Defer the `TORCH_MAJOR`/`TORCH_MINOR` import in `op_builder/xpu/builder.py` from the module header into `version_dependent_macros()` with a try/except fallback, so importing the builder no longer triggers an ImportError when torch is not yet installed. Issue #4984 reported that `pip install deepspeed==0.13.0` fails during metadata preparation with `ImportError: cannot import name 'TORCH_MAJOR' from 'op_builder.builder'`, because the xpu builder module eagerly imported torch-dependent symbols at import time. Since torch is not declared as a build requirement, the import fails before installation can complete. By deferring these imports to the methods that actually need them, the package can be imported and installed without torch present, restoring the pre-0.13.0 install behavior.

context.issue:
Issue #4944: [BUG] Setting Finetune=True causes checkpoint loading to not work correctly
Using GPT-NeoX (which uses DeepSpeed), we noticed that with `finetune: True`, DeepSpeed is somehow incorrectly loading the checkpoint.  We think it has something to do with module vs. optimizer parameters not being updated (or tied) correctly, similarly described in this [issue](https://github.com/EleutherAI/gpt-neox/pull/927).  Supposedly this was fixed with pull requests, but I think it broke again at some point.

We were able to pinpoint this bug to happen between DeepSpeed version 0.10.0 (works ok), and 0.10.2 (which has this bug).  Specifically, we tested this by using the `finetune` flag like a resume function, where we set the learning rate to be the same as where pretraining left off.  We would expect the loss to be in range as during pretraining. (With `finetune=True`, the only difference from resuming pretraining is that the optimizer states are not loaded, but we set the learning rate to be there same as where it left off).

What happens instead is, the very first step (step 0) is close where pretraining left off, but then the next step it jumps super high, and then tapers down (not fully recovering), but basically behaves like it is training from scratch there after.  This happens in newer DeepSpeed versions.

Using the older DeepSpeed version 0.10.0 avoids this behavior, and the loss starts off and stays inline with pretraining, ie continuing to improve.  When I upgrade to anything after this version (0.10.2+), I get the bug.

I am using Torch 2.0, Cuda 11.7, on Ubuntu 22.04.

Has anybody had issue with finetune settings using DeepSpeed?  Thanks!

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix checkpoint loading when finetune=True by preventing optimizer state restoration

Fix a bug where setting `finetune=True` caused incorrect checkpoint loading behavior. When `finetune=True` (which sets `load_optimizer_states=False` and `load_module_only=True`), the code was incorrectly loading zero checkpoint optimizer states and calling `_restore_from_bit16_weights()`, causing the model to behave as if training from scratch after the first step.

The fix ensures that:
1. Zero checkpoint loading is skipped when `load_optimizer_states=False` or `load_module_only=True`
2. `refresh_fp32_params()` is called for all optimizer types when `load_module_only=True`, not just when fp16 is enabled

This aligns the behavior with DeepSpeed 0.10.0 where finetune/resume functionality worked correctly.
messages.claude:
fix: skip loading zero optimizer states when finetune (load_module_only) to prevent training instability

When `finetune=True` (module-only loading), DeepSpeed was incorrectly loading ZeRO optimizer states from the checkpoint, causing the optimizer to resume with stale state that didn't match the freshly loaded module weights. This produced the loss spike and training-from-scratch behavior reported in #4944 (regression introduced between 0.10.0 and 0.10.2): step 0 looked fine because the module weights were correct, but the optimizer state (momentum, variance) was inconsistent with the new weights, so subsequent steps diverged.

The fix decouples `load_zero_checkpoint` from `load_optimizer_states` and gates the actual ZeRO state load behind `load_optimizer_states and not load_module_only`. When finetuning, the ZeRO load is skipped (success=False), forcing `_restore_from_bit16_weights` to rebuild a clean optimizer state. Also unconditionally refreshes fp32 params on module-only load (not just for fp16), so bf16/ZeRO paths correctly restore the master weights before optimizer state is rebuilt.

Refs #4944
messages.minimax:
fix: correct checkpoint loading when finetune=True

When `finetune=True`, `load_optimizer_states` is set to False, which caused two issues:

1. Zero checkpoint loading was being skipped entirely even when bfloat16 was enabled, preventing proper fp32 parameter restoration. The fix removes `load_optimizer_states` from the guard condition so zero checkpoints are loaded based on `load_path` and optimization mode alone.

2. The `refresh_fp32_params()` call was guarded by `fp16_enabled()`, but this method is also needed for bfloat16 to restore tied/inverted weights correctly. Removing this check ensures fp32 parameters are refreshed in all precision modes.

Without these fixes, fine-tuning produced incorrect behavior where step 0 was correct but subsequent steps behaved as if training from scratch, due to stale fp32 parameters not being restored.

messages.kimi:
fix: Clean up gradient accumulation hooks and debug module names on destroy

What:
- Add `destroy()` method to ZeRO Stage 1/2 optimizer to remove gradient accumulation hooks
- Track gradient accumulation hooks in `_grad_acc_hooks` list in both Stage 1/2 and Stage 3
- Add `debug_clear_module_and_param_names()` function and call it in engine's `destroy()` method

Why:
When using DeepSpeed ZeRO optimizer, GPU memory was not being released after training completed because gradient accumulation hooks retained references to model parameters. This caused memory leaks when users needed to free GPU memory for subsequent operations (e.g., merging LoRA adapters). The fix properly removes all gradient hooks during cleanup and clears debug module/param name caches to ensure complete resource release.
messages.claude:
fix: clear gradient accumulation hooks and debug caches on engine destroy to resolve ZeRO memory leak

What:
- Track gradient accumulator hooks registered via `register_hook` in ZeRO stage 1/2 (`stage_1_and_2.py`) and stage 3 (`stage3.py`) by storing them in `self._grad_acc_hooks`.
- Add `destroy()` in `stage_1_and_2.py` and extend the existing `destroy()` in `stage3.py` to call `hook.remove()` on each registered hook before tearing down the offload/buffers.
- Add `debug_clear_module_and_param_names()` in `deepspeed/utils/debug.py` to reset the global `module_names`/`param_names` dicts.
- Invoke `debug_clear_module_and_param_names()` from `DeepSpeedEngine.destroy()` so debug name caches are released alongside the optimizer.

Why:
- Issue #4856 reports that GPU memory is not released after training finishes when using ZeRO Stage 2 (and similarly Stage 3), even after explicit `gc.collect()` / `torch.cuda.empty_cache()`. This blocks subsequent steps in the same process that need GPU memory (e.g. reloading a model to merge LoRA adapters).
- Root cause: the backward hooks registered on gradient accumulators (`grad_acc.register_hook(...)`) keep references that prevent the model parameters and optimizer state from being garbage-collected. The hooks were never removed during shutdown, so the param tensors and associated buffers stayed alive on the GPU.
- By collecting the returned hook handles at registration time and removing them in `destroy()`, the references held by the autograd graph are released, allowing Python/Torch to free the parameter and optimizer memory. The same applies to the debug module/param name dicts in `utils/debug.py`, which otherwise retain references to model structure indefinitely.
- This makes `DeepSpeedEngine.destroy()` (and the ZeRO optimizers' `destroy()`) actually reclaim memory, matching the user expectation in the issue that cleanup after `trainer.train()` should free the GPU for downstream work.
messages.minimax:
fix: clean up gradient accumulation hooks and debug state on destroy to prevent memory leak

The bug report shows GPU memory not being released after training with ZeRO Stage 2, while normal DDP cleans up correctly. Root cause: gradient accumulation hooks registered via `register_hook()` were never removed, and global debug dictionaries (`module_names`, `param_names`) were never cleared.

Changes:
- Store registered hooks in `self._grad_acc_hooks` list in both Stage3 and Stage1And2
- Remove hooks in `destroy()` by iterating and calling `hook.remove()`
- Add `debug_clear_module_and_param_names()` to reset global debug state
- Call debug cleanup in engine `destroy()` method

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix recursive module duration calculation in FlopsProfiler

Change `get_module_duration()` to recursively call itself when summing child module durations, instead of directly accessing `__duration__`. This fixes a ZeroDivisionError that occurred when profiling models with nested submodules (like AV-HuBERT), where the parent module's duration was incorrectly reported as zero because child durations weren't being properly accumulated. The fix aligns `get_module_duration()` with the existing behavior of `get_module_macs()` and `get_module_flops()`.
messages.claude:
fix: recurse into child modules in get_module_duration

The FlopsProfiler's get_module_duration() only summed the immediate
children's __duration__, which fails for nested module hierarchies
(e.g. AV-HuBERT) where intermediate children also have duration == 0.
The un-recurse leaves total duration at 0, producing a
ZeroDivisionError in print_model_profile when computing flops per
second (flops / fwd_latency).

This makes get_module_duration consistent with get_module_macs and
get_module_flops, both of which already recurse into child modules.
Replacing the direct attribute access m.__duration__ with a recursive
call to get_module_duration(m) ensures durations are accumulated
correctly at all nesting depths.

Fixes #4334.
messages.minimax:
fix: make get_module_duration recursively calculate duration for nested modules

The get_module_duration() function was not recursing into child modules when summing up duration, causing a ZeroDivisionError when profiling models with multiple levels of submodules (e.g., nested ModuleList). Unlike get_module_macs() and get_module_flops() which properly recurse, get_module_duration() directly accessed __duration__ on child modules, missing deeper descendants. This fix changes the function to recursively call itself, consistent with the other profiler functions.

Issue #4507: [BUG] gemm_test uses rocblas instead of hipblas, but dose not include rocblas
With rocm 5.7 deepspeed no longer compiles as rocblas is use directly here:
https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed/blob/4fc181b01077521ba42379013ce91a1c294e5d8e/csrc/includes/gemm_test.h#L68
instead of hipblas.

hipify translates to, and will only include, hip headers and thus this will fail to compile.
Previously in AMD's rocm implementation of hip, rocblas was indirectly included here, this is no longer the case in 5.7, thus any translation unit with this header in it will fail to compile

additionally __HIP_PLATFORM_HCC__ is deprecated and should be replaced with __HIP_PLATFORM_AMD__ in code paths that are intended to target the rocm hip implementation only

messages.kimi:
fix: Add missing rocblas header include for HIP platform compatibility

Add explicit `#include <rocblas/rocblas.h>` when `__HIP_PLATFORM_HCC__` is defined in `gemm_test.h`. This resolves compilation failures on ROCm 5.7+ where rocblas is used directly but was previously only indirectly included through hip headers. The change ensures compatibility with newer ROCm versions that no longer provide transitive rocblas includes.
messages.claude:
build: include rocblas header in gemm_test.h for ROCm 5.7 compatibility

With ROCm 5.7, the indirect inclusion of rocblas via hip headers no longer happens, causing compilation failures in translation units that include gemm_test.h. hipify only translates to hip headers, so the rocblas symbols referenced in gemm_test.h (e.g., for GEMM testing) remain unresolved without an explicit include. This addresses the build break reported in issue #4507 and the broader ROCm build warnings surfaced in issue #4513 by guarding the rocblas include behind __HIP_PLATFORM_HCC__ so non-ROCm builds are unaffected.
messages.minimax:
fix: add missing rocblas include for HIP platform compilation

When compiling with ROCM 5.7+, the rocblas headers are no longer indirectly included in gemm_test.h, causing compilation failures. This change adds the explicit rocblas include under __HIP_PLATFORM_HCC__ to fix the build issue.

fix: preserve existing PDSH_SSH_ARGS_APPEND values when setting SSH port

Change the assignment operator from `=` to `+=` when setting `PDSH_SSH_ARGS_APPEND` to ensure any user-defined values in the environment are preserved rather than overwritten. messages.kimi:
fix: Fix MoE checkpoint loading when optimizer state files are missing with load_optimizer_states=False

The bug occurred because the code attempted to load optimizer checkpoint files for MoE models even when `load_optimizer_states=False`. This caused a `FileNotFoundError` when the `optim_state` files were missing or intentionally excluded.

The fix restructures the logic in `_load_checkpoint()` to only load optimizer checkpoint files when `load_optimizer_states=True`. The optimizer checkpoint loading is now properly guarded by the `load_optimizer_states` condition, and `optim_checkpoint` is only populated when actually needed. This allows users to load checkpoints without optimizer state files while still being able to load other states like the LR scheduler.
messages.claude:
fix: skip loading optimizer checkpoint files when load_optimizer_states=False

What:
- Restructure `_load_checkpoint` in `deepspeed/runtime/engine.py` so that
  optimizer checkpoint files for MoE models are only loaded when
  `load_optimizer_states` is actually True. Previously the MoE optim file
  was loaded unconditionally whenever `load_module_only` was False, even
  when the caller did not request optimizer states.
- Gate the `optim_checkpoint` assignment behind the
  `load_optimizer_states and not has_zero_optimizer_state` branch, and
  only fetch the expert-parallel optim file inside that branch for MoE
  models.
- Replace the final `client_state['optimizer']` injection condition from
  `not load_optimizer_states and not load_module_only` to
  `optim_checkpoint is not None`, so the optimizer tensor is only placed
  into client_state when it was genuinely loaded. This also enables the
  bfloat16 path to use `load_state_dict` with
  `load_optimizer_states=load_optimizer_states`.
- Add a regression test in `tests/unit/checkpoint/common.py` that patches
  `_get_optimizer_ckpt_name` to assert it is never called when
  `load_optimizer_states=False`, ensuring no optim file is read from disk.

Why:
- Fixes #2737. When loading a DeepSpeed checkpoint for an MoE model with
  `load_optimizer_states=False`, the engine still attempted to read the
  per-expert-rank `*_optim_states.pt` file from disk. If that file was
  intentionally or accidentally missing (e.g. only module + LR scheduler
  states were saved, or the optim files were deleted), the load failed
  with `FileNotFoundError` at engine.py:2843.
- The previous workaround was `load_module_only=True`, but that is too
  coarse: it also skips LR scheduler state restoration, which users may
  still want. The fix decouples "load optimizer states" from "load
  module only" so callers can omit optimizer files while still loading
  the scheduler.
- The bug was caused by two issues: (1) the MoE optim-file load was
  placed outside the `load_optimizer_states` guard, so it ran regardless
  of the flag; (2) the final `client_state` injection used the wrong
  condition, which would either drop the optimizer tensor or inject it
  even when nothing was loaded. Moving the load inside the
  `load_optimizer_states` branch and keying the injection on
  `optim_checkpoint is not None` makes `client_state` correctly reflect
  what was actually loaded, matching the issue's expected behavior.
messages.minimax:
fix: tolerate missing optim_state files when load_optimizer_states=False for MoE

When loading MoE checkpoints with load_optimizer_states=False, the code was still attempting to load optim_state files which could be intentionally or accidentally missing, causing FileNotFoundError. This fix ensures the optimizer checkpoint is only loaded when load_optimizer_states=True, and client_state is only populated with optimizer state when it was actually loaded.

    "train_micro_batch_size_per_gpu": 2,
    "zero_allow_untested_optimizer": True,

model = ModelWithSharedWeights()
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

fix: Fix shared weights detection in ZeRO-2 checkpoints

Fix a bug where `_get_shared_params()` incorrectly used `param.ds_id` for all models, causing shared weights to be missing when reconstructing state dicts from ZeRO-2 checkpoints. The fix adds a check to determine if the model is using ZeRO-3 (where `ds_id` is available and unique) versus ZeRO-2 (where we must fall back to `param.data_ptr()`). This ensures shared weight layers are properly tracked and included in the checkpoint conversion output.
messages.claude:
fix: support shared weights in ZeRO-2 checkpoint reconstruction

What:
- Modify `_get_shared_params` in `deepspeed/runtime/engine.py` to detect shared
  parameters for both ZeRO-2 and ZeRO-3 stages. Instead of relying solely on
  `param.ds_id` (which only exists for ZeRO-3-managed parameters), fall back to
  `param.data_ptr()` when the engine is not running ZeRO-3 weight partitioning.
- Add a new test `tests/unit/checkpoint/test_shared_weights.py` covering the
  scenario where two linear layers tie their weights under a ZeRO-2 config and
  verifying that `get_fp32_state_dict_from_zero_checkpoint` returns a state
  dict that loads with `strict=True`.

Why:
- Issue #3824 reports that reconstructing full weights from a ZeRO-2 checkpoint
  fails with a "Missing key(s) in state_dict" error when layers share (tie)
  weights. The root cause is that `_get_shared_params` unconditionally checked
  for `param.ds_id` to identify shared parameters. ZeRO-2 does not assign
  `ds_id` to parameters (only ZeRO-3 does), so the function skipped all
  parameters, dropped the shared-weight mapping, and the resulting state dict
  was missing the tied parameter entry (e.g. `layer2.weight`).
- With this change, the engine detects whether it is operating under ZeRO-3
  weight partitioning (`zero_optimization_partition_weights()` plus presence of
  `ds_id`) and, for non-ZeRO-3 cases, uses `data_ptr()` as the unique parameter
  identifier to correctly record shared parameters. This restores the shared
  parameter map for ZeRO-2 checkpoints so the reconstruction utility emits a
  complete state dict and `model.load_state_dict(..., strict=True)` succeeds.
- The added unit test reproduces the original bug report's scenario and guards
  against regressions of shared-weight handling under ZeRO-2.
messages.minimax:
fix: correctly detect shared weights in ZeRO-2 checkpoints

When loading ZeRO-2 checkpoints via get_fp32_state_dict_from_zero_checkpoint, layers with shared weights were incorrectly reconstructed, causing missing key errors. The shared params detection relied on param.ds_id, which is only available in ZeRO-3. This caused the fallback to param.data_ptr() to incorrectly identify shared weights in ZeRO-2 models. The fix introduces an is_zero3_model check to use ds_id for ZeRO-3 and data_ptr() for ZeRO-2, ensuring correct shared weight reconstruction across both optimization stages.

messages.claude:
fix: handle attention_mask correctly in inference softmax kernels

Previously, the inference kernels mishandled HuggingFace attention masks, causing masked padding tokens to dramatically shift outputs (e.g., 0.25 max logit difference vs. 0.00011 without DeepSpeed). The root cause was threefold: (1) the softmax kernel applied the mask only when `!triangular` was true, which skipped masking for causal-LM models where `triangular_masking` is set; (2) mask offset indexing used the wrong vector lane (`high_data[i].y` instead of `high_data[i].x` for the third element), corrupting the attention probabilities; and (3) `launch_attn_softmax_v2` passed `heads * batch_size` as the heads count unconditionally, which is only correct under triangular masking.

This change removes the `!triangular` condition from the mask application in both fp16 and fp32 softmax kernels, fixes the lane assignment for the third mask element, and threads the `triangular` flag through to the launch site so the heads count is computed correctly. The mask pointer is now passed through as an `at::Tensor&` from the Python binding down to `ds_softmax`/`attention_unfused`, replacing the raw `T*` parameter so the masking status can be inferred from the tensor's rank at the call site rather than being dropped at the boundary.

Additionally, the `encoder_decoder` config flag (which conflated "is a HuggingFace model" with "return a tuple") is renamed to `return_tuple` to reflect its actual purpose, and the fp16 path no longer upcasts to fp32 when `triangular_masking` is false, which was masking the underlying kernel bug at the cost of correctness. The `-1 * std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity()` sentinel is replaced with `-10000.0` to match HF's mask scaling convention and avoid NaN propagation in fp16.
messages.kimi:
fix: Correct attention mask handling in inference kernels for Huggingface compatibility

This commit fixes a bug where DeepSpeed's inference kernels incorrectly handled Huggingface-style attention masks, causing significant output differences when padding tokens were present. The changes address several issues:

1. Fixed mask pointer handling: Changed `attn_mask_ptr` from raw pointer to `at::Tensor&` reference in `ds_softmax` and `attention_unfused` functions, with proper null-checking based on tensor dimensions rather than boolean flags.

2. Corrected mask application logic: Removed the `!triangular` condition from mask application in `attn_softmax_v2` kernel, ensuring masks are always applied when `recompute` is true. Also fixed a typo where `high_data[i].y` was incorrectly used instead of `high_data[i].x`.

3. Fixed minus_infinity constant: Changed from `-1 * std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity()` to `-10000.0` to avoid potential CUDA numerical issues.

4. Unified return type handling: Replaced the `encoder_decoder` flag with a more general `return_tuple` parameter across the inference engine, module injection, and transformer configurations. This properly handles Huggingface models that expect tuple outputs.

5. Simplified attention mask flow: Removed conditional float conversion and triangular masking checks that were incorrectly filtering mask applications, ensuring consistent mask handling regardless of attention type.

These changes ensure that padded tokens are properly masked out during inference, preventing them from affecting the attention computation and producing incorrect logits.

Key changes:
- softmax.cu: Removed incorrect `!triangular` check so mask is always applied during recompute; fixed high_data[i].x assignment bug; changed minus_infinity to -10000.0 for compatibility; adjusted heads parameter calculation for triangular case
- pt_binding.cpp: Changed attn_mask parameter from raw pointer to tensor reference; pass mask tensor directly to kernel
- transformer_inference.py: Simplified no_masking logic to always pass input_mask; updated return_tuple handling

Issue #1978: DeepSpeed Inference support for OPT
Right now OPT (https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/opt) can only be supported via custom kernel injection policy. It would be great if there's official support. Thanks!

messages.claude:
feat: add DeepSpeed inference support for HuggingFace OPT models

What:
- Add new HFOPTLayerPolicy in replace_policy.py covering both 125m-style (pre-attention norm) and 350m-style (post-attention norm) OPT variants, and register it in the replace_policies list.
- Introduce ActivationFuncType enum (deepspeed/utils/types.py) and thread it from policy -> config -> op builder -> CUDA kernel, so MLP can dispatch between GELU and ReLU; add a fused bias+ReLU CUDA kernel (relu.cu) with fp32/fp16 templates and bind it via pt_binding.cpp.
- Generalize layer-norm placement: replace the hard-coded `preln` boolean threaded through replace_module.py with policy-driven `pre_attn_norm`, and expose `mlp_act_func_type` on DeepSpeedInferenceConfig so each model family controls its own norm order and activation.
- Fix K/V cache tensor layout in ds_softmax_context to be reshaped as [bsz, heads, all_tokens, k] (head-grouped) instead of [bsz, all_tokens, hidden_dim], matching what consumers expect.
- Propagate the HF model config into DSPolicy (engine.py) so policies can read model-specific attributes at injection time.
- Add OPT models to tests/unit/inference/test_inference.py.

Why:
- Issue #1978 requests official DeepSpeed inference support for HuggingFace OPT, which currently only works via a custom injection policy. OPT uses ReLU (not GELU) in its MLP and, for the 350m variant, applies layer norm after attention rather than before — both diverge from the BERT/GPT assumptions baked into the existing inference path.
- The previous code hard-coded GELU and a BERT-style `preln=True/False` switch tied to HFBertLayerPolicy, making it impossible to correctly express OPT's activation and norm placement. Moving both attributes onto the policy class lets each model family declare its own behavior (OPT-125m sets pre_attn_norm=True + ReLU; OPT-350m sets pre_attn_norm=False + ReLU) without special-casing in the replacement logic.
- The K/V cache reshape fix corrects a latent shape bug that surfaced when exercising OPT's attention path; the previous [bsz, all_tokens, hidden_dim] layout did not expose the head dimension needed by downstream consumers.
- The added fused bias+ReLU kernel mirrors the existing fused bias+GELU path so ReLU models get the same fused-kernel performance rather than falling back to an unfused emission.
- Adding OPT models to the inference test suite guards against regressions for both norm-placement variants going forward.

feat(checkpoint): Add clone_tensors_for_torch_save utility to prevent ZeRO checkpoint bloat

Adds a new utility function `clone_tensors_for_torch_save()` that clones tensors before saving to prevent checkpoint size inflation. When using ZeRO stage 1 and 2, `torch.save()` saves the underlying storage of flattened tensors rather than just the slice, causing checkpoint sizes to balloon (e.g., 26GB → 76GB). The utility recursively clones tensors and moves them to a specified device (default CPU), ensuring only the actual tensor data is saved. Includes documentation update and unit tests covering ZeRO stages 1 and 2 with both CPU and accelerator devices.
messages.claude:
feat: add clone_tensors_for_torch_save utility to avoid ZeRO checkpoint bloat

What:
Add a new `clone_tensors_for_torch_save` helper in `deepspeed/checkpoint/utils.py` that recursively clones tensors (and tensors nested inside lists, tuples, and dicts) onto a target device before they are handed to `torch.save()`. Document the utility in `docs/code-docs/source/model-checkpointing.rst` with a HuggingFace usage example, and cover it with a new `TestSaveTensorClone` distributed test in `tests/unit/checkpoint/test_zero_optimizer.py` that verifies both CPU and accelerator target devices across ZeRO stages 1 and 2.

Why:
Fixes #3303, where model checkpoints saved via `model.save_pretrained()` ballooned in size (e.g. 26G -> 76G for llama-7b) after `deepspeed.initialize` under ZeRO stage 1/2. The root cause is the interaction between ZeRO's tensor flattening — which allocates model tensors as slices of large contiguous flat buffers — and PyTorch's serialization behavior, which by default saves the entire underlying storage of a tensor rather than only the slice that corresponds to the individual tensor (see https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/serialization.html#preserve-storage-sharing). As a result, every parameter that shares a flat buffer drags the full buffer into the checkpoint, multiplying the on-disk size.

Cloning each tensor before `torch.save()` produces a new storage sized to the actual tensor, so only the real parameter bytes are written. The helper centralizes this pattern (previously users had to hand-roll a dict comprehension of `v.clone()`) and handles nested containers so it can be applied directly to a `state_dict()`. The cloned storage is reclaimed by the garbage collector after saving, so memory bloat during the save itself is transient. The new test guards against regressions by saving the same state dict with and without cloning and confirming the loaded tensors still match.
messages.minimax:

The fix clones tensors before saving so the storage matches the logical tensor size, which the garbage collector then reclaims to avoid memory bloat. Cloning is applied recursively to tensors nested in lists, tuples, and dicts. Fixes issue #3303.

messages.kimi:
fix: correct parameter assignment in copy_data_to_new_module for GPT-J inference

The copy_data_to_new_module method was incorrectly assigning parameters by directly setting dst = src when src was None, which didn't actually modify the module attributes. This caused GPT-J inference with kernel inject to fail because the attention norm weights (attn_nw, attn_nb) and input norm weights (norm_w, norm_b) weren't being properly copied to the new module.

The fix uses setattr to properly assign None values when parameters don't exist, and wraps non-None parameters in torch.nn.parameter.Parameter before copying to the accelerator device. This ensures the module attributes are actually updated regardless of whether the source is None or a tensor. The test file change re-enables the GPT-J-6B model in inference tests since this fix resolves the underlying issue.
messages.claude:
fix: resolve GPT-J kernel injection failure by properly setting module parameters

The previous copy_data_to_new_module implementation built a dict keyed
by the *current* parameter tensors (self.module.mlp.attn_nw, etc.) and
then assigned to the loop variable `dst` instead of the actual module
attribute. This meant the source values were never written back onto the
module, so when any of attn_nw/attn_nb/norm_w/norm_b was None the target
parameter silently kept its stale/initialized value rather than being
cleared. The result was that GPT-J inference with kernel inject read
incorrect weights and failed at runtime (issue #3604), while other
models happened to pass because their parameters were non-None and the
broken copy path was masked.

Rework the routine to iterate over attribute-name strings and use
setattr() so the assignment actually lands on the module:
- For attn_nw / attn_nb, write onto self.module.mlp.
- For norm_w / norm_b, write onto self.module.
- When the source is None, set the attribute to None instead of
  assigning to a throwaway loop variable.
- When the source is present, wrap it in a
  torch.nn.parameter.Parameter and move it to the current accelerator
  device, preserving the previous tensor-copy intent but through a
  correct assignment path.

Also re-enable the EleutherAI/gpt-j-6B entry in
tests/unit/inference/test_inference.py that had been disabled due to
random OOM errors. Bringing it back is what surfaced this regression in
the first place — without it the broken copy path went unnoticed on
master. A TODO is left noting the OOM issue still needs a follow-up.
messages.minimax:

Issue #3408: [BUG] Local rank mismatch error when training on nodes with different number of GPUs
**Describe the bug**
When training Megatron-DeepSpeed models on nodes with different number of GPUs (e.g., node 0: 2 GPUs, node 1: 4 GPUs), local rank mismatch error (`AssertionError: expected local-rank to be the same as rank % device-count.`) occurs in https://github.com/microsoft/Megatron-DeepSpeed/blob/main/megatron/initialize.py#L207. 

I found that this is caused by local ranks set by DeepSpeed launcher **mismatching** the local ranks set by Megatron-DeepSpeed.
Specifically, while DeepSpeed assigns local ranks corresponding to global ranks sequentially (e.g., global ranks: [2, 3, 4, 5] -> local ranks: [0, 1, 2, 3]), Megatron-DeepSpeed decides each local rank as **global rank % device count of the node** (e.g., global ranks: [2, 3, 4, 5] -> local ranks: [2, 3, 0, 1]).

2. Prepare a cluster where each node has different number of GPUs (e.g., two nodes each with 2 and 4 GPUs, respectively).
3. Execute a training script.

**Expected behavior**
Training starts normally without an error in such setup. Because DeepSpeed document does not restrict that all nodes must be homogeneous (i.e., exacltly the same number of GPUs), I expected training to work properly for clusters where nodes have different number of GPUs.

messages.kimi:
fix: correct local rank calculation for heterogeneous GPU nodes

The DeepSpeed launcher was assigning local ranks sequentially (0, 1, 2, 3) based on iteration order, but Megatron-DeepSpeed and PyTorch expect local ranks to be calculated as `global_rank % num_local_devices`. This caused an assertion error when training on nodes with different numbers of GPUs (e.g., node 0 with 2 GPUs, node 1 with 4 GPUs).

Changed the local rank assignment from sequential iteration index to `dist_rank % num_local_procs` to align with the expected behavior and enable training on heterogeneous GPU configurations.

Fixes #3408
messages.claude:
fix: correct local rank assignment for nodes with different GPU counts

What:
In `deepspeed/launcher/launch.py`, change the launcher to compute each
process's `LOCAL_RANK` as `dist_rank % num_local_procs` instead of using
the loop index of the local process enumeration. The loop variable is
renamed from `local_rank` to `local_proc` to avoid shadowing the real
local rank, and `local_rank` is now derived from the global rank.

Why:
When training on heterogeneous clusters (e.g., node 0 with 2 GPUs and
node 1 with 4 GPUs), DeepSpeed assigned local ranks by simply
enumerating processes sequentially per node. Downstream frameworks such
as Megatron-DeepSpeed, however, define local rank as
`global_rank % device_count_of_node` (see issue #3408). This caused the
launcher-emitted `LOCAL_RANK` to mismatch the framework's expected
value, triggering
`AssertionError: expected local-rank to be the same as rank % device-count.`
at Megatron initialization.

Computing `LOCAL_RANK` as `dist_rank % num_local_procs` aligns the
launcher's local rank semantics with the `global_rank % device_count`
convention used by consumers, so training can start normally on clusters
where nodes have different numbers of GPUs.

What:

- Remove top-level torch import from transformer_inference.py
- Add try/except block in is_compatible() method to handle missing torch import gracefully

Why:
DeepSpeed 0.7.0 broke Accelerate CI because pip installing deepspeed alongside torch (via `pip install -e .[testing]`) failed during compilation. The transformer_inference builder was importing torch at module level, causing ImportError during pip install before torch was actually available. This fix allows DeepSpeed to be installed without torch being pre-installed, deferring the torch dependency check to runtime when the builder's is_compatible() method is called.

Move the `import torch` call inside `is_compatible()` of the transformer
inference op builder into a try/except block, returning False (with a
warning) when torch is not yet installed. Previously the import lived at
module top-level, so merely importing the builder during `pip install`
required torch to already be present in the environment.

This fixes the installation regression reported in #2166, where DeepSpeed
0.7.0 breaks Accelerate's CI (and any user running `pip install -e

collects deepspeed before torch is installed, the setup hook imports the

formatting CI workflow, since torch is no longer needed there and the

Looking at the code changes and the related issue, I can see this is a bug fix for an infinite recursion error that occurs when `deepspeed.zero.Init` context wraps both the model creation and the `deepspeed.initialize` call.

The fix:
1. Extracts the cleanup logic from `__exit__` into a new `shutdown_init_context()` function
2. Adds a global `zero_init_enabled` flag to track if the context is active
3. Calls `shutdown_init_context()` at the start of `deepspeed.initialize()` to disable the zero.Init context if it's currently enabled
4. Also includes a minor fix for CUDA version parsing (removing `packaging` dependency)

The issue is that when `zero.Init` context wraps `deepspeed.initialize()`, the patched torch functions cause infinite recursion. The fix ensures the zero.Init context is properly shut down before deepspeed.initialize runs.

fix: Disable zero.Init context before deepspeed.initialize to prevent infinite recursion

When deepspeed.zero.Init context wraps both model creation and deepspeed.initialize(), the patched torch functions cause a RecursionError. This worked in 0.6.4 but broke in 0.6.5.

Changes:
- Extract cleanup logic from Init.__exit__ into new shutdown_init_context() function
- Add zero_init_enabled global flag to track context state
- Call shutdown_init_context() at start of deepspeed.initialize() to disable any active zero.Init context
- Fix CUDA version parsing to use string split instead of packaging.version

This allows Lightning Lite and similar integrations to wrap the entire run() method with zero.Init context without encountering infinite recursion errors (fixes #2139).
messages.claude:
fix: resolve infinite recursion when zero.Init context wraps deepspeed.initialize

What:
- Extract the zero.Init teardown logic from `__exit__` into a new standalone
  `shutdown_init_context()` function in `partition_parameters.py`
- Add a module-level `zero_init_enabled` flag so the teardown is idempotent
  and a no-op when the context was never entered
- Call `shutdown_init_context()` at the start of `deepspeed.initialize()` to
  forcibly disable the zero.Init context if it is still active
- Remove the `packaging.version` dependency in
  `op_builder/transformer_inference.py`, replacing it with a simple
  `int(torch.version.cuda.split('.')[0])` parse
- Add `test_ds_init_w_zinit` to verify the recursion error no longer occurs
  when the context wraps the `deepspeed.initialize` call

Why:
Issue #2139 reports a RecursionError raised when `deepspeed.zero.Init` wraps
not only the model construction but also the `deepspeed.initialize()` call.
This was a regression introduced in 0.6.5 (worked in 0.6.4) and blocks the
integration with Lightning Lite, which wraps the entire run() method (model
creation + initialize) inside the zero.Init context. The recursion happens
because, during `initialize()`, DeepSpeed internally constructs modules
(e.g. for the engine/optimizer wrappers). With the patched
`torch.nn.Module.__init_subclass__`/`__init__` hooks still installed, each
new module instantiation re-enters the partitioning logic, which in turn
creates more modules, leading to unbounded recursion. Shutting down the
context before any internal module construction in `initialize()` ensures
the hooks are removed and subsequent module creation behaves normally. The
teardown was refactored into a reusable function so it can be invoked both
from `__exit__` (the normal path) and from `initialize()` (the fallback
path) without duplicating the restoration logic. The idempotent flag
guarantees that calling `shutdown_init_context()` when zero.Init was never
enabled is a safe no-op, so users who do not wrap `initialize()` are
unaffected. The `packaging` import removal is a small drive-by cleanup to
drop an unnecessary third-party dependency for a trivial version parse.
messages.minimax:
fix: prevent infinite recursion when deepspeed.zero.Init wraps deepspeed.initialize

The zero.Init context was causing infinite recursion when it wrapped both the model and the deepspeed.initialize call, a regression from 0.6.4. This occurred because __exit__ would reset torch monkey-patches while the context was still active, leading to recursive re-entry during deepspeed.initialize. The fix introduces a zero_init_enabled flag to track context state, extracts the reset logic into shutdown_init_context(), and calls it at the start of deepspeed.initialize to cleanly disengage any active zero.Init context before proceeding. Also removes an unnecessary packaging.version import and fixes a minor CUDA version parsing issue.

fix: Add torch.cuda.is_available() check before calling is_bf16_supported()

The prebuild process fails when cross-compiling on a VM without GPUs because torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() raises a RuntimeError when no CUDA GPUs are available. This prevents users from preparing Docker images for CI environments that lack GPUs.

Add torch.cuda.is_available() to the existing hasattr check to ensure bf16 support detection only occurs when CUDA is actually available, allowing prebuilding to succeed in GPU-less environments.
messages.claude:
fix: allow prebuild on machines without GPUs

Guard the bf16 support detection in setup.py with torch.cuda.is_available() so
that torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() is only invoked when a CUDA device is
actually present.

Previously, setup.py unconditionally called torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()
whenever the attribute existed on the torch version. On a GPU-less build host
(e.g., a CI VM used for cross-compiling), this call traverses into
torch.cuda.current_device() -> _lazy_init() -> torch._C._cuda_init(), which
raises `RuntimeError: No CUDA GPUs are available` and aborts the build before
any op can be compiled.

This blocks the workflow of prebuilding DeepSpeed ops on a GPU-free machine
for later use on GPU-enabled machines (e.g., preparing docker images for CI).
Adding the is_available() short-circuit lets the build proceed on CPU-only
hosts while preserving the existing bf16 detection behavior when GPUs are
available, resolving issue #2010.
messages.minimax:
fix: add torch.cuda.is_available() check before calling is_bf16_supported()

Prevents RuntimeError when prebuilding on machines without GPUs (e.g., CPU-only CI VMs or cross-compilation environments). The torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() function calls torch.cuda.current_device() internally which fails if no CUDA devices are available. Adding the availability check allows the prebuild to proceed gracefully on CPU-only machines.

messages.claude:
fix: lazy import fcntl to avoid ImportError on Windows

The `fcntl` module is Unix-only and unavailable on Windows, causing
`ImportError: No module named 'fcntl'` when importing
`deepspeed.utils.debug` on Windows platforms (issue #1905). Windows
users reported the package failing to import on Windows 11 / Python 3.7
since the module-level `import fcntl` executed unconditionally.

inside `printflock()` (via `print_rank_0`). The module-level import is
replaced with `fcntl = None`, and a lazy import is performed on first

without error; the fcntl-based file locking will only be invoked when
`printflock()` is actually called (primarily on Linux), where the import
will succeed.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix NameError when torch is not installed during deepspeed setup

The bug occurs because TORCH_MAJOR and TORCH_MINOR variables are defined unconditionally at module level in builder.py, but the torch import is wrapped in a try-except block that only prints a warning on ImportError. When torch is not installed, the import fails but the code continues to execute TORCH_MAJOR = int(torch.__version__.split('.')[0]), causing a NameError.

The fix moves TORCH_MAJOR and TORCH_MINOR definitions into an else block after the try-except, ensuring they are only defined when torch is successfully imported. Additionally, the is_rocm_pytorch() method is updated to handle the case where torch is not available by wrapping the torch import in a nested try-except block. Redundant torch imports are also removed from fused_adam.py, fused_lamb.py, and transformer.py since they already import from builder.py.

This resolves Issue #1865 where installing deepspeed>=0.6 without tensorflow (or in a fresh virtual environment) would fail with NameError during setup.
messages.claude:
fix: resolve NameError when torch not installed during deepspeed setup

Guard the TORCH_MAJOR/TORCH_MINOR version parsing with the existing
`else` branch of the torch import try/except in op_builder/builder.py,
so the module-level code no longer references `torch` when the import
failed. Also wrap the torch usage inside `is_rocm_pytorch()` in its own
try/except and remove the now-redundant top-level `import torch` from
fused_adam.py, fused_lamb.py, and transformer.py.

Why: Since v0.6.0, installing deepspeed (e.g. via `pip install
deepspeed==0.6.0`) crashed with `NameError: name 'torch' is not
defined` whenever torch was absent from the environment, even though
the code already printed a warning intended to allow op-builder to be
imported without torch (issue #1865). The warning logic was bypassed
because the version-parsing lines executed unconditionally right after
the failed import, breaking metadata generation during pip install and
blocking installation alongside packages like tensorflow in a fresh
virtualenv.
messages.minimax:

from fused_adam, fused_lamb, and transformer modules.

fix: Set default CUDA device in Zero3 parameter initialization to prevent NCCL duplicate GPU error

Add `torch.cuda.set_device(self.local_device)` after determining the local device in Zero3's parameter partitioning initialization. This fixes the NCCL "Duplicate GPU detected" error that occurs when multiple ranks attempt to use the same CUDA device because the default device was not properly set before distributed operations. The issue manifested as invalid NCCL usage during model loading with ZeRO stage 3, where ranks 0 and 1 were both detected on the same CUDA device due to missing device context setup.
messages.claude:
fix: set default CUDA device to local device in ZeroInit

Explicitly call torch.cuda.set_device() with the local device after
deriving it from LOCAL_RANK during parameter partition initialization.

Previously, Init() only recorded self.local_device but never set it as
the default CUDA device. When DeepSpeed was used outside of a training
loop that sets the device (e.g., loading a pretrained model under
Zero3 via HfDeepSpeedConfig), every rank defaulted to CUDA device 0.
This caused NCCL to detect duplicate GPUs across ranks
("Duplicate GPU detected : rank 0 and rank 1 both on CUDA device 0")
and ultimately fail with ncclInvalidUsage, since collective operations
like all_gather were issued on the wrong device/stream.

Setting the default device early in Init() ensures each rank operates
on its assigned GPU, which is required for NCCL collectives to work
correctly.

Fixes #1604

messages.kimi:
fix: prevent local tmp directory creation during ds_report execution

The `has_function()` method in `op_builder/builder.py` was creating local directories (e.g., `tmp` on Linux, `var` on macOS) when compiling test files. This occurred because `distutils.ccompiler.CCompiler.object_filenames()` uses the source file's directory as the default output location when no `output_dir` is specified.

The fix extracts the root directory from the absolute path of the temporary source file and passes it explicitly as `output_dir`, ensuring compiled objects are placed in the intended temp directory and properly cleaned up after execution.
messages.claude:
fix: prevent local tmp/var directory creation during op compilation

When compiling C test programs in has_function(), distutils'
CCompiler.object_filenames() derives output paths from the source file's
location when no output_dir is provided. Because the source file lives in
a tempdir, distutils falls back to writing the resulting object files into
a local tmp/ (Linux) or var/ (macOS) directory relative to the current
working directory. These leftover directories were never cleaned up,
leaving stray artifacts after `ds_report` (and during installation).

Compute an explicit output_dir from the source filename's drive and
absolute path so the object files land inside the intended tempdir rather
than the cwd. This sidesteps the distutils behavior without monkeypatching
it, ensuring no temporary local directories remain after execution
(issue #1493).
messages.minimax:
fix: specify output_dir to prevent temp directory left behind after compilation

When compiling C programs via distutils, object files were being written to a local directory
(tmp on Linux, var on macOS) instead of the system temp directory. This happened because
distutils.ccompiler.CCompiler.object_filenames() defaults to a local directory when output_dir
is not explicitly provided. The workaround explicitly computes and passes output_dir based on
the source filename's drive and root components, ensuring object files use the temp directory
and are cleaned up properly after execution.

context.issue:
Issue #332: ZeRO checkpointing to support torch.optim.Adam
ZeRO checkpointing currently works only for apex's fused_adam, but not for torch's adam.

messages.claude:
fix: enable ZeRO checkpointing support for torch.optim.Adam

What:
- Remove the separate `TORCH_ADAM_OPTIMIZER` optimizer type and merge its behavior into the generic `ADAM_OPTIMIZER` path. When `ADAM_OPTIMIZER` is selected, use `torch.optim.Adam` if ZeRO CPU offload is enabled, and `apex.FusedAdam` otherwise.
- Drop the special-case assertions in `DeepSpeedConfig` that forced `TORCH_ADAM_OPTIMIZER` to require ZeRO + CPU offload, and remove the dedicated untested-optimizer warnings for ZeRO-Offload now that torch Adam is routed through the standard Adam branch.
- Make the ZeRO optimizer state handling tensor-aware so non-tensor state entries (e.g. `torch.optim.Adam`'s scalar `step`) are passed through untouched: `async_copy_to` returns non-tensor/non-container values as-is; `_get_state_without_padding` and `_restore_base_optimizer_state` copy only tensor state and assign scalars directly; `_partition_base_optimizer_state` skips flatten/alignment for non-tensor partitions.
- Remove a stray `state_dict = None` that discarded the freshly async-copied checkpoint state.
- Update unit tests (`test_checkpointing.py`, `test_fp16.py`) to drop the `optimizer_type` parameter and hard-code `"Adam"`, covering both non-offload (FusedAdam) and CPU-offload (torch Adam) paths under ZeRO stage 1/2.

Why:
- Resolves issue #332: ZeRO checkpointing previously worked only for apex's FusedAdam and silently mishandled `torch.optim.Adam`, whose optimizer state contains a non-tensor `step` entry. The old code assumed every state value was a tensor, so flattening, padding-stripping, and `copy_` calls crashed or corrupted state for torch Adam.
- The dedicated `torch_adam` type was redundant once the only real difference (CPU-offload routing) could be selected automatically based on `zero_cpu_offload()`. context.issue:
Issue #407: Pipeline throughput is incorrect
I think the throughput should be ```tput = self.train_batch_size() * self.steps_per_print() / elapsed ```. Right now it is not taking into account the logging frequency.

https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed/blob/4ac9bf60a740a5a8433ee256c48527c0fba63beb/deepspeed/runtime/pipe/engine.py#L277

messages.kimi:
fix: Correct pipeline throughput calculation in train_batch

The throughput calculation was using `elapsed` time directly instead of accounting for the logging frequency (`steps_per_print`). This caused incorrect throughput values to be reported.

The fix changes the calculation from:
  `tput = train_batch_size() / elapsed`
to:
  `tput = train_batch_size() / iter_time`
where `iter_time = elapsed / steps_per_print()`

This ensures throughput accurately reflects samples processed per second across all steps in the logging interval, not just per elapsed second.

Fixes #407
messages.claude:
fix: correct pipeline throughput calculation to account for logging frequency

What:
- Reorder `self.timers('train_batch').start()` to just before the training schedule is constructed and executed, so the measured `elapsed` time accurately reflects only the training work.
- Compute `tput` as `self.train_batch_size() / iter_time` instead of `self.train_batch_size() / elapsed`, where `iter_time = elapsed / self.steps_per_print()`.

Why:
- The reported throughput was wrong because it divided `train_batch_size()` by the full `elapsed` time of a `train_batch` call, without accounting for the logging frequency (`steps_per_print`). Per issue #407, the expected throughput is `train_batch_size() * steps_per_print / elapsed`, which is algebraically equivalent to `train_batch_size() / (elapsed / steps_per_print)` = `train_batch_size() / iter_time`.
- Separately, the timer was started before an intervening comment/blank line and the schedule setup, which inflated `elapsed` with non-training work; moving `start()` to immediately precede the actual work keeps the measurement honest, ensuring `iter_time` (and therefore `tput`) is computed against time actually spent training.
messages.minimax:
fix: correct pipeline throughput calculation to account for logging frequency

The throughput metric was incorrectly calculated as train_batch_size / elapsed,
which doesn't account for the logging interval. When steps_per_print > 1, the
reported throughput was inflated because it was dividing by wall-clock time
for multiple iterations rather than per-iteration time.

Now calculates iter_time = elapsed / steps_per_print(), then derives
throughput = train_batch_size / iter_time, which is equivalent to
train_batch_size * steps_per_print() / elapsed and matches the correct
throughput the issue requested.

feat: Add Python 3.14 compatibility layer for annotation handling

Add deepspeed/compat.py with get_annotations() and get_annotations_from_namespace() functions to handle PEP 649/749 annotation changes in Python 3.14+. Update layer_container_base.py and parameter_base.py to use these compatibility functions instead of direct __annotations__ access. This fixes the MoE layer import error (Issue #7673) where annotations were not being properly retrieved from class namespaces, causing "Target parameter not found" and "Must have wildcard in source name" ValueErrors when importing deepspeed.layer.moe.
messages.claude:
fix: support Python 3.14 annotation handling in inference layer containers

What:
- Add deepspeed/compat.py with get_annotations_from_namespace() and
  get_annotations() helpers that wrap the new annotationlib module
  (Python >=3.14) and fall back to __annotations__ on older versions.
- Replace direct attrs.get("__annotations__", {}) and obj.__annotations__
  accesses in LayerMetaclass/ParameterMetaclass
  (layer_container_base.py, parameter_base.py) with the new helpers.

Why:
- Issue #7673 reports that importing deepspeed.moe.layer on current
  master raises ValueError "Target parameter 'qkv_w' not found in this
  layer" (and the ParametrizedList wildcard error), making the MoE layer
  unusable.
- Root cause: the metaclasses rely on attrs["__annotations__"] and
  instance.__annotations__, but under PEP 649/749 (default in Python
  3.14) annotations are no longer eagerly materialized on the namespace;
  they are computed lazily via the __annotate__ protocol. The old access
  pattern therefore returns an empty dict, so LayerMetaclass sees no
  declared parameters and the dependency-mapping validation fails.
- The new helpers detect annotationlib when available and use
  get_annotate_from_class_namespace / call_annotate_function to retrieve
  the real annotation dict, restoring the pre-3.14 behavior where
  parameter groups and their dependencies are correctly discovered.
- Falling back to obj.__annotations__ keeps older Python versions (and
  non-class objects) working unchanged, so the fix is backward
  compatible while unblocking DeepSpeed on Python 3.14.

pr_title: Enable control over timeout with environment variable

context.issue:
Issue #3905: [REQUEST] Add timeout as entry-point option or environment variable
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
I am using Hugging Face `transformers` for my deep learning, and it has a nice option to restrict specific processing to the main process only. This is useful if a function caches the result: the main process does the processing while the other processes wait, and when main is done, the other processes can just load from the cache. That's pretty neat.

The problem arises when these are long running processes. In distributed environment (torch or deepspeed, for instance), the communication between processes has a default timeout. If no communication has occurred for `timeout` seconds, the whole program will exit. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Both [`torch`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#torch.distributed.init_process_group) and [`deepspeed`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#torch.distributed.init_process_group) provide options in the Python init methods to set the timeout parameter to a higher value than the default 30 minutes, but this option is not available from the command-line or through an environment, which is what I would like.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I could make a custom fork but I think that this is something that more people might need as soon as they scale to larger projects.

**Additional context**

I can work on this, depending on what you suggest as a solution (CLI argument for the `deepspeed` command or as environment variable).

feat: allow default process group timeout to be set via environment variable

The default process group timeout was hardcoded to 30 minutes, which is too
short for long-running distributed workloads. Users running DeepSpeed under
frameworks like Hugging Face `transformers` often perform main-process-only
work (e.g. result caching) that can exceed this window with no inter-process
communication, causing the program to exit prematurely.

Both `torch.distributed` and `deepspeed.init_distributed` expose a timeout
parameter in their Python init methods, but there was no way to override it
from the command line or environment. This meant users hitting the limit had
to either monkey-patch the constant or maintain a custom fork (issue #3905).

Read the timeout from the `DEEPSPEED_TIMEOUT` environment variable (in
minutes), defaulting to 30 to preserve the previous behavior. This gives
operators a zero-code knob to extend the timeout for large-scale jobs while
keeping the existing default intact.

fix: Remove deprecated torch._six import to support PyTorch 2.0+

PyTorch 2.0 removed the torch._six module (pytorch/pytorch#94709), causing ModuleNotFoundError when importing inf from torch._six. This change adds a compatibility fallback to import inf directly from torch when torch._six is unavailable, ensuring DeepSpeed works with both older and newer PyTorch versions. The fix centralizes the inf import in runtime/utils.py and updates all dependent modules (stage3.py, stage_1_and_2.py) to import from the common location.
messages.claude:
fix: replace removed torch._six import with fallback to torch.inf

PyTorch 2.0 removed the torch._six module (pytorch/pytorch#94709), causing
DeepSpeed to crash at import time with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
'torch._six'` on newer torch builds (issue #2845).

What:
- Wrap the `from torch._six import inf` import in utils.py with a try/except
  that falls back to `from torch import inf` when torch._six is unavailable.
- Re-export `inf` from utils.py and update stage3.py and stage_1_and_2.py to
  import it from there instead of directly from torch._six.

Why:
- torch._six was a PyTorch internal shim module that has been removed in
  PyTorch 2.0.0a0. `inf` is now available directly under the top-level
  `torch` namespace, so the fallback preserves identical behavior across
  both old and new torch versions.
- Centralizing the import in utils.py (rather than adding try/except in each
  consumer) avoids duplicating the compatibility shim across the three files
  that previously imported from torch._six, and gives a single place to
  update if the import path changes again.

feat: Add CPU Adagrad optimizer implementation

Add DeepSpeedCPUAdagrad optimizer following the DeepSpeedCPUAdam pattern to enable CPU offloading for Adagrad optimizer. This implementation includes AVX SIMD optimizations (AVX512/AVX2), half-precision support, and sparse gradient handling. The optimizer reduces GPU memory usage by keeping optimizer states on CPU while maintaining performance through optimized CPU kernels. Also refactors CPU Adam to use common utilities and adds comprehensive unit tests for correctness verification against PyTorch's native Adagrad.

feat: add CPU Adagrad optimizer with AVX/SIMD support

What
- Add csrc/adagrad/cpu_adagrad.cpp implementing the Adagrad_Optimizer
  with Step_1/Step_4/Step_8 variants and the AVX vectorized fast path,
  mirroring the structure of the existing cpu_adam implementation.

pr_title: Add assert to ensure we don't skip unsupported grad dtypes

context.issue:
Issue #1416: [BUG] EmbeddingBag sparse gradients skipped without error or warning
**Describe the bug**
When you try to use `EmbeddingBag` with sparse gradients, they will be skipped silently and will not be used in `all_reduce` logic because [`split_half_float_double_csr`](https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed/blob/master/deepspeed/runtime/engine.py#L79) doesn't check `torch.cuda.sparse.FloatTensor` type.
I think we need to change logic and not iterate over data types, but rather iterate over tensors and check that their data type in supported data types.

**To Reproduce**
```python
import copy
import torch
import typing
import torch.distributed
import deepspeed

params = {
    "train_batch_size": 2048,
    "train_micro_batch_size_per_gpu": 1024,
    "steps_per_print": 1,
    "sparse_gradients": True,
}


class Adam(torch.optim.Optimizer):
    def __init__(
        self,
        dense_params: list,
        sparse_params: list,
        lr: float = 1e-3,
        betas: typing.Tuple[float, float] = (0.9, 0.999),
        eps: float = 1e-8,
        weight_decay: float = 0,
        amsgrad: bool = False,
    ):
        super().__init__(
            dense_params + sparse_params, dict(lr=lr, betas=betas, eps=eps, weight_decay=weight_decay, amsgrad=amsgrad)
        )

        self.adam = torch.optim.Adam(dense_params, lr, betas, eps, weight_decay, amsgrad)
        self.adam_sparse = torch.optim.SparseAdam(sparse_params, lr, betas, eps)

    def state_dict(self) -> dict:
        result = super().state_dict()
        result["adam"] = self.adam.state_dict()
        result["adam_sparse"] = self.adam_sparse.state_dict()
        return result

    def load_state_dict(self, state_dict: dict) -> None:
        state_dict = copy.deepcopy(state_dict)
        self.adam.load_state_dict(state_dict.pop("adam"))
        self.adam_sparse.load_state_dict(state_dict.pop("adam_sparse"))
        super().load_state_dict(state_dict)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def step(self, closure=None) -> typing.Optional[float]:
        loss_1 = self.adam.step(closure)
        loss_2 = self.adam_sparse.step(closure)

        if loss_1 is not None and loss_2 is not None:
            return loss_1 + loss_2
        return loss_1 or loss_2


class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = torch.nn.EmbeddingBag(10, 3, mode="sum", sparse=True)
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(3, 1)

    def forward(self, x, offsets):
        return self.linear(self.emb(x, offsets))

fix: Add assertion for unsupported gradient types in split_half_float_double_csr

Add explicit assertion to fail fast when encountering unsupported gradient tensor types during allreduce operations. Previously, sparse gradients from EmbeddingBag were silently skipped without error or warning, causing silent correctness issues. The fix validates each tensor type against supported types (Half, Float, Double, CSR) and raises AssertionError with clear message if unsupported type is found.

Also includes:
- Code cleanup: remove unused loop variable, clean up commented code
- Documentation update: mark sparse_gradients feature as deprecated
- Test: add unit test verifying assertion is raised for sparse gradients
- Test infrastructure: disable NCCL_DEBUG logging in distributed tests

Fixes #1416
messages.claude:
fix: validate gradient types in split_half_float_double_csr to surface unsupported sparse tensors

What:
- Add an assertion in `split_half_float_double_csr` that checks each tensor's type against the supported types list, raising a clear error when an unsupported type (e.g. `torch.cuda.sparse.FloatTensor` from `EmbeddingBag` with `sparse=True`) is encountered.
- Rename `dtypes` to `supported_types` for clarity and drop the unused loop index in `buffered_allreduce_fallback`.
- Remove stale `TODO` comments and dead commented-out code around the CSR/allreduce bucketing paths.
- Mark the `sparse_gradients` config option as essentially deprecated and incompatible with `torch.sparse` features in the config docs.
- Silence `NCCL_DEBUG` in the unit test harness to reduce log noise.
- Add `tests/unit/test_sparse_grads.py` reproducing the EmbeddingBag sparse-gradient scenario and asserting the new error is raised.

Why:
Issue #1416 reported that `EmbeddingBag` sparse gradients were silently skipped during `all_reduce` because `split_half_float_double_csr` iterated over a fixed list of dtype strings and never matched `torch.cuda.sparse.FloatTensor`. As a result, sparse gradients were dropped without any warning, leading to silent training corruption that was extremely hard to diagnose. As suggested in the issue, the iteration is now driven by the tensors themselves, validating each one against the supported set so any unsupported gradient type fails fast with an actionable message instead of being ignored. The deprecation note and test pin this behavior going forward.
messages.minimax:
fix: add explicit type assertion for sparse gradients in allreduce

The `split_half_float_double_csr` function was silently skipping sparse gradient tensors (e.g., `torch.cuda.sparse.FloatTensor` from `EmbeddingBag`) because it only iterated over dense CUDA tensor types, causing sparse gradients to be dropped without error or warning during allreduce operations. This fix adds an explicit assertion that validates each tensor's type against the supported types list before bucketing, providing a clear error message when an unsupported grad type is encountered. Additionally, removed dead TODO comments, cleaned up unused loop variables, and improved code formatting. The sparse_gradients feature documentation has been updated to note it is essentially deprecated and incompatible with `torch.sparse` features. A test has been added to verify that using sparse gradients with an unsupported optimizer raises an AssertionError.

fix: Add guard check in BF16_Optimizer.destroy() to prevent IndexError with DummyOptim

When DeepSpeed is initialized with `optimizer=None` (which creates `DummyOptim`) and BF16 enabled, calling `engine.destroy()` raises an `IndexError` because `BF16_Optimizer.destroy()` unconditionally iterates over `bf16_groups` even when `using_real_optimizer == False` and `bf16_groups` is empty. This fix adds an early return check at the beginning of the `destroy()` method to skip the cleanup logic when no real optimizer is being used, preventing the IndexError when accessing empty `bf16_groups`.

fix: guard BF16_Optimizer.destroy() early return when using DummyOptim

When DeepSpeed is initialized with optimizer=None (DummyOptim) and BF16 enabled, calling engine.destroy() raises an IndexError because destroy() unconditionally iterates over bf16_groups which remains empty when using_real_optimizer is False. messages.claude:
fix: prevent IndexError in BF16_Optimizer.destroy() when using DummyOptim

When DeepSpeed is initialized with optimizer=None, a DummyOptim is created
and BF16_Optimizer is set up with using_real_optimizer=False, leaving
bf16_groups empty. The destroy() method unconditionally iterated over
self.optimizer.param_groups and indexed self.bf16_groups[i], which raised
an IndexError because bf16_groups has no entries in this dummy case.

This caused engine.destroy() to crash during teardown for users running
BF16-enabled inference or training without supplying a real optimizer
(see Issue #7752), a valid and supported configuration.

Guard the teardown by returning early from destroy() when
using_real_optimizer is False, so the bf16_groups cleanup is skipped
for the dummy path where those buffers were never allocated.

messages.claude:
feat: extend offload_states/reload_states to support ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2

What:
- Remove the ZeRO-3-only assertions in `deepspeed/runtime/engine.py` `offload_states`/`reload_states` so ZeRO stages 1 and 2 are no longer blocked.
- Implement `offload_states` and `reload_states` on `DeepSpeedZeroOptimizer` in `deepspeed/runtime/zero/stage_1_and_2.py`, covering HP params, LP params, LP grads, and optimizer states, with pin_memory/non_blocking support and an `offloaded_states` set to track what has been moved.
- Add generic `offload_optimizer_states`/`reload_optimizer_states` helpers in `deepspeed/runtime/zero/offload_states.py` to move optimizer state tensors across devices without assuming DeepSpeed Adam's structure.
- Add `_clear_hp_buffer_references`/`_clear_lp_params_references` to release gradient views, HP-mapping fragments, and optimizer fragments so GPU memory is actually freed before offload, followed by gc + empty_cache.
- Extend `tests/unit/runtime/zero/test_offload_states.py` with ZeRO-1/2 coverage (`TestOffloadStatesZero12`, `run_model_zero12`) and rename the ZeRO-3 path to `TestOffloadStatesZero3`/`run_model_zero3`.

Why:
Issue #7251 reports that `offload_states`/`reload_states` only worked under ZeRO-3 due to hard assertions, so frameworks like OpenRLHF — which combine Adam state offload/reload with auto tensor parallelism for RL training — could not use ZeRO-2. ZeRO-1/2 keep LP params sharded on GPU and only shard optimizer/HP state, so the existing ZeRO-3 implementation could not be reused directly: it was necessary to clear references that pin GPU memory (grad buffers, `_hp_mapping` fragments) before moving tensors, to reconstruct `parallel_partitioned_bit16_groups` on reload, to preserve the `averaged_gradients` dict structure so gradients can be reloaded in place, and to use a structure-agnostic optimizer-state mover instead of the Adam-specific `offload_adam_states`. The `offloaded_states` set enables selective, idempotent offload of individual state types (matching the `include` argument already used by ZeRO-3) and ensures reload only restores what was actually moved.

fix: Use accelerator device for straggler all_reduce tensors in comms logging

The straggler calculation in `log_all()` was creating tensors on CPU by default, causing `RuntimeError: No backend type associated with device type cpu` when using NCCL backend with GPUs. The fix retrieves the current accelerator device and creates `lats` and `min_lats` tensors on the correct device, ensuring the all_reduce operation works correctly with the configured backend.
messages.claude:
fix: place straggler all-reduce tensors on the accelerator device in comms logging

What:
- In `deepspeed/utils/comms_logging.py::log_all`, fetch the current device via
  `get_accelerator().current_device_name()` and pass it as the `device` argument
  when constructing `lats` and `min_lats` tensors used for the straggler
  all-reduce. Both tensors are now created on the accelerator device instead of
  the default CPU.

Why:
- Issue #7397 reports a runtime crash when enabling straggler reporting with the
  NCCL backend. NCCL only supports GPU tensors, but the straggler tensors were
  being allocated on CPU, so `dist.all_reduce(min_lats, op=ReduceOp.MIN)` failed
  with `RuntimeError: No backend type associated with device type cpu`.
- DeepSpeed's accelerator abstraction layer determines the active backend/device
  combination at runtime; certain ops (such as all-reduce under NCCL) are only
  valid on GPU tensors. Hardcoding CPU placement ignored this constraint and made
  `deepspeed.comm.log_summary(show_straggler=True)` unusable on GPU/NCCL setups.
- By sourcing the device from `get_accelerator()`, the tensors are placed on the
  same device as the model and communicator, so the MIN all-reduce and the
  derived `total_straggler` calculation run against the correct backend. This
  makes straggler reporting work for the common GPU+NCCL configuration while
  remaining compatible with other accelerator/backends through the abstraction
  layer, rather than assuming CPU as the previous code did.

fix: guard contiguous grad buffer offload against None buffer

messages.kimi:
fix: Conditionally quote environment variables in multinode_runner to fix MPI training

The add_export method was unconditionally quoting all environment variable values, which broke module imports when PYTHONPATH was wrapped in quotes (e.g., "/usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages" instead of /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages). This regression was introduced in commit fc22d960 after version 0.15.2.

Changed the logic to only quote values containing special shell characters (anything outside [\w@%+=:,./-]), ensuring that simple paths remain unquoted while values like "64(x2)" are properly quoted to avoid bash syntax errors. Added unit tests to verify both cases.
messages.claude:
fix: only quote env var exports when they contain special characters

The previous behavior (introduced in fc22d960) unconditionally wrapped every
exported environment variable in double quotes. This breaks MPI-based training
when the value is a path like PYTHONPATH: the shell ends up with a quoted
"(some path)", which Python cannot import from, so module imports fail.

Issue #6997 reports that module imports break under MPI because PYTHONPATH gets
exported as a quoted string. The root cause is that quoting is only required for
values containing shell-special characters (e.g., parentheses in SLURM_JOB_CPUS_PER_NODE
values like "64(x2)"); plain paths and other safe tokens must remain unquoted.

What:
- Add a regex check in MultiNodeRunner.add_export that only wraps the value in
  double quotes when it contains characters outside the safe set
  [\w@%+=:,./-]. Values composed entirely of safe characters are stored as-is.
- Add unit tests (DummyRunner subclass of MultiNodeRunner) covering both the
  special-character case (quoted) and the plain-path case (unquoted).

Why:
- Fix the regression where PYTHONPATH and similar path-based env vars were being
  quoted unnecessarily, breaking module imports under MPI.
- Preserve correct shell escaping for values that genuinely need it (e.g.,
  SLURM_JOB_CPUS_PER_NODE with parentheses), avoiding bash syntax errors.

fix: correct attribute name in start_time_hook duplicate registration check

The flops_profiler's `start_time_hook` was checking `hasattr(module, "__start_time_hook_handle")` (single trailing underscore) while the attribute is actually registered as `__start_time_hook_handle__` (double trailing underscores). By aligning the attribute name in the guard with the one actually being set, the duplicate-registration check now works as intended: the hook (and its closure) is registered only once per module, so `torch.save` succeeds after `get_model_profile`. Fixes #5432.

feat: Add CUDA compute capability 9.0 support to fix kernel execution on Hopper GPUs

The change adds compute capability 9.0 (Hopper architecture, e.g., H100) to the default compute capabilities list. Without this, users on Hopper GPUs encounter "no kernel image is available for execution on the device" errors because the build system wasn't including sm_90 kernels. image was compiled for sm_90 GPUs (e.g. Hopper). As a result, users on
Hopper-class GPUs hit "CUDA error: no kernel image is available for

PTX/SASS for compute_90 so that Hopper devices receive a usable kernel
image at install time, resolving the runtime error.
